newsitem.title: USA: Hubble crew ends shuttle mission with night touchdown.
newsitem.headline: Hubble crew ends shuttle mission with night touchdown.

text.p: The space shuttle Discovery streaked like a comet across the pre-dawn sky on Friday, landing in Florida after refurbishing the Hubble Space Telescope.

The $2 billion reusable spaceship swooped out of a star-filled sky and touched down at 3:32 a.m. EST (0832 GMT) on the Kennedy Space Center's 3-mile-long (5-km-long) runway in a rare nighttime landing.
Shuttle skipper Ken Bowersox was guided by the light of the nearly full moon, banks of powerful search lights and a newly installed stretch of lamps down the centre of the runway.
"You have this yellow brick road right out in front of you," Bowersox said. "You just keep the orbiter going right down the yellow brick road."
The 100-ton shuttle drifted in the darkness before touchdown, landing on the right side of the 300-foot-wide (91-metre-wide) runway.
"That drift you saw there is exactly why we have those centre-line lights," Bowersox said at a news conference. "I was really glad to have them."
Shuttle commanders requested the new lights because it is difficult in the dark to line up the shuttle for a perfect touchdown.

The gliding shuttle touches down at nearly twice the speed of a conventional airliner and there is little room for error. The shuttle landing strip is surrounded by ditches and alligator-infested swamps.

Of the 82 shuttle missions, only nine have ended in darkness, but NASA expects nighttime and low-light dawn landings to become more commonplace once it starts assembly of its international space station.
The shuttle's fiery re-entry left a blazing trail in the sky above Texas as it hurtled through the atmosphere at 10,500 mph (16,900 kph).
A television camera atop the mission control building in Houston captured its glowing streak as it passed the moon, heading out across the Gulf of Mexico.
"You lit up the entire sky with the orbiter and its trail," Kevin Kregel radioed from mission control. "It was pretty impressive."
Eyewitnesses at NASA's Johnson Space Centre said the shuttle's orange-tinged trail hung in the air for several minutes, stretching from horizon to horizon.
"It looked like someone had taken an orange magic marker and drew across the sky," one observer said.
Bad weather at the Kennedy Space Centre had kept Discovery aloft for one more orbit of Earth. Clouds cleared just in time for the shuttle's last Florida landing opportunity on Friday.
The shuttle had left the spaceport before dawn on Feb. 11 for a $350 million overhaul of the Hubble Space Telescope.
Two teams of spacewalking astronauts made five spacewalks to refurbish and upgrade the orbiting observatory. They installed two new instruments and eight other upgraded components.
Astronomers expected to get the first images and data in May from the telescope's new multipurpose infrared camera and improved light-splitting spectrograph.
"Although our part of it is done, I will be eagerly awaiting those first verification images to make sure everything went well," said Discovery crewman Steve Hawley, a former astronomer.
NASA's next shuttle mission, a 16-day research flight by Columbia, was scheduled for launch on April 3.
